title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — foedus naturae invents supernatural; before Secunda
pass_a_gloss: For the rest I would gladly inquire whence the learned man had it that by the covenant of nature, whose condition was natural justice, supernatural justice had been promised? Does Scripture say that anywhere? Or can it be gathered by reasoning from contemplation of Nature? I ask also whence he had it that Adam, who was from the earth, earthly, and whose paradise was on earth, did not have the earth as homeland? He certainly seems to remove the distinction between the covenant of nature and the covenant of grace, the first man and the second, and to teach something, indeed to invent a certain will and promise of God beyond Scripture. Which every Christian, especially a professor of Theology among the Reformed, must avoid with utmost care.
pass_b_english: Beyond that I would gladly know Garissoles' source for saying the covenant of nature—conditioned on natural justice—promised supernatural justice. Where does Scripture say so? Can bare contemplation of nature prove it by reasoning?

And where did he get the claim that Adam—earthly, from the earth, with an earthly paradise—did not have earth for his homeland? That erases the line between nature's covenant and grace's, between the first man and the second, and invents a divine will and promise beyond Scripture. No Christian—least of all a Reformed professor of theology—may risk that.
source_text: Ceterum libenter quaesiverim, unde habuerit Vir Doctus foedere naturae, cuius conditio fuit justitia naturalis, promissam fuisse justitiam supernaturalem? Id ne alicubi dicit Scriptura? An potest ratiocinando ex Naturae contemplatione colligi? Quaero etiam unde habuerit, Adami, qui e terra fuit, terrenus, & cuius paradisus fuit in terra, patriam non fuisse terram? Tollere certe videtur discrimen inter foedus naturae & foedus gratiae, primum hominem & secundum, & aliquid docere, immo Dei voluntatem quandam & promissionem confingere praeter Scripturam. Id quod omni Christiano, praecipue inter Reformatos Theologiae professori summa cura vitandum est.
